title: How 600 Men Toppled an Empire
description: The paradox of Spanish conquest: how disease, Native alliances, and technology — not guns alone — toppled the Mexica and Inca empires.
essential_question: How did a few hundred Spaniards topple empires of millions?
learning_objectives: Explain why guns alone cannot account for Spanish victories.
Identify the roles of smallpox, the Tlaxcalans, and steel and horses in the conquests.
Compare the falls of Tenochtitlan (1521) and the Inca state (1532-33) as one pattern.

key_terms.definition: Spanish conquerors who toppled the Mexica and Inca empires in the 1500s.
An Afro-Eurasian disease that devastated Indigenous populations lacking immunity.
Enemies of the Mexica who allied with Cortés, supplying tens of thousands of warriors.

narration.text: Cusco was the capital of an empire that ruled millions, stretching from the Andes to the sea. [beat] In 1533 [emphasis]a few hundred Spaniards[/emphasis] seized it. Just as [es]Cortés[/es] had toppled the [es]Mexica[/es] empire a decade earlier. Guns alone cannot explain this. [urgent] So how did a few hundred men conquer worlds of millions?

narration.text: Smallpox traveled ahead of the armies and [emphasis]killed far more people[/emphasis] than any battle. The [es]Tlaxcalans[/es], enemies of the [es]Mexica[/es], sent tens of thousands of warriors to fight beside [es]Cortés[/es]. Horses and steel gave the Spanish an edge in close combat. [beat] Victory was a system: [fast]disease, alliances, and technology working together[/fast].

bullets: Disease first: smallpox killed more than any battle
Alliances: the Tlaxcalans sent tens of thousands of warriors
Edges, not miracles: steel swords and horses in close combat
Victory was a system — disease, alliances, technology

narration.text: [es]Cortés[/es] reached [es]Tenochtitlan[/es] in 1519 and found an empire strained by tribute and rivalries he learned to exploit. [beat] After smallpox ravaged the city, his coalition took it in 1521. A decade later [es]Pizarro[/es] copied the formula in Peru: [emphasis]seize the emperor [es]Atahualpa[/es] in 1532[/emphasis], and the Inca state fractured. Two empires, one pattern.

events: Cortés lands in Mexico; learns Mexica rivalries
Smallpox ravages Tenochtitlan during the siege
Pizarro seizes Atahualpa; the Inca state fractures

narration.text: [slow]Conquest was not the end of the story. It was the foundation of everything that followed.[/slow] Spanish rule replaced tribute empires with colonial labor systems. The mines, the sugar plantations, and the flow of goods across the Atlantic all rested on what the [es]conquistadors[/es] had seized. [emphasis]To understand the exchange, start with the conquest.[/emphasis]
